title: Pain the medicine
hook: pain became the medicine and pleasure the disease (Asa di Var, ang 469)

segments.voice: Yesterday, when the heart is true, and your line: a true heart. Did you do your one true thing? Yesterday's salok ended with truth as medicine. Today's turns the medicine upside down. Day five hundred fifty.

Ask people when they changed the most, and very few will say it was the year everything went well. They'll name the breakup, the layoff, the hospital waiting room, the year a parent died. Nobody would choose those seasons. Nobody should wish them on anyone. And yet, looking back, many people say: that's when I woke up. That's when I found out who my friends were, or what I actually believed. Guru Nanak put that strange experience into one line of the Asa di Var, and it still startles people who hear it.
screen: `WHEN DID YOU CHANGE THE MOST?` → `NOBODY CHOOSES THOSE SEASONS.` → `ONE STARTLING LINE.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 469. Its opening line, in paraphrase: pain has become the medicine, and pleasure the disease, because where there is pleasure, there is no longing for you. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog. Dukh is pain, sorrow, suffering. Daaroo is medicine. Sukh is comfort, pleasure, ease. Rog is disease. It's worth slowing down, because this line is easy to misread. Guru Nanak isn't saying pain is good, or that people deserve to suffer, or that anyone should go looking for it. Sikh teaching doesn't praise hurting yourself; the Gurus turned away from harsh self-punishment as a path. And in Sikh life, relieving other people's pain is a duty: the langar feeds the hungry, and Sikhs have long run free kitchens and clinics in disasters. The line is about what comfort can do to the heart. When everything is easy, it's easy to forget the One. Ease can make us sleepy. Pain, the salok says, often does the opposite. It breaks the illusion that we're in control, and it turns the heart toward the One. Then the salok goes on, still in paraphrase: you are the Doer; I am nothing; if I try to do it myself, nothing happens. And then a line that connects back to day five hundred forty-two: I am a sacrifice to you, dwelling in your kudrat, your creation; your limits can't be known. So the medicine isn't the pain itself. It's what pain can open: the end of pretending we run the world, and a turn toward the One who does.
screen: `DUKH DAAROO, SUKH ROG.` · `NOT: PAIN IS GOOD.` · `EASE CAN MAKE US FORGET.` · `YOU ARE THE DOER.` · then, large: `PAIN THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a lesson in one pain. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of a hard season that is now behind you, not the hardest, and not one that still feels raw. If nothing comes, that's fine; just rest in the breath. If one does come, don't relive it. Ask one quiet question: what did that season teach me, or turn me toward? Let the answer be small. A friendship. A habit. A kind of patience. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, for what you learned and for who helped. The bell holds the time.
Pain the medicine. Dukh daaroo, sukh rog: in Guru Nanak's salok, pain can turn the heart toward the One, while ease can make it forget.

Your line: pain the medicine. Today, if something small goes wrong, ask what it's pointing you toward before you push it away. And if someone near you is hurting, be part of their medicine. Day five hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and many recall dukh daaroo, sukh rog in hard times as a reminder that suffering can turn the heart toward the One.

fork.setup: life has been easy for months, and you've stopped thinking about the One. what does the salok call that ease?
fork.reveal: dukh daaroo, sukh rog: pain became the medicine, pleasure the disease, because in pleasure there's no longing for the One.

original.note: Gurmukhi: pain the medicine, pleasure the disease; the opening of the salok.

trapdoor: what you thought: suffering is good for you.
what it means: ease can make the heart forget the One; pain can break the illusion of control and turn it back.
what a scholar hears: dukh and sukh trade places with daaroo and rog; the salok goes on to 'you are the Doer' and a sacrifice to the One in kudrat.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (dukh daaroo sukh rog bhaiaa), Ang 469

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the line 'jaa sukh taam na hoee' rendered as 'where there is pleasure there is no longing for you', and the following lines (you are the Doer; if I try nothing happens; balihaaree kudrat vasiaa; your limits can't be known).
Care taken not to glorify suffering; confirm the statement that the Gurus turned away from harsh self-punishment and that relieving others' pain is a duty in Sikh life.
Free kitchens and clinics in disasters are mentioned generally; no organization named.
